answer: A tenant improvement allowance is money a landlord puts toward renovating leased space, usually a set amount per square foot. Who pays for the rest depends on the lease: an allowance, a turnkey build or a landlord-delivered shell plus an allowance. Settle the amount, what it covers and who pays overruns before signing.

blocks.x: Tenant improvements (TIs) are the renovations that turn a raw or previously used commercial space into a space that works for a new tenant. In Winnipeg's office, retail and medical markets, the TI package can help decide whether a lease gets signed. The tenant improvement allowance is often a key number in that negotiation.
What counts as a tenant improvement?
Anything that adapts the space to the tenant's use:
New walls, offices, meeting rooms and reception areas
Flooring, ceilings, paint and lighting
Washrooms, kitchenettes and break rooms
Electrical and data for workstations and equipment
HVAC changes for new room layouts
Specialty items: exam rooms, sinks, storage, display fixtures
Who pays: three common tenant improvement allowance structures

blocks.x: [BDC's guide to commercial leasing terms](https://www.bdc.ca/en/articles-tools/money-finance/buy-lease-commercial-real-estate/13-terms-you-need-to-understand-before-signing-your-commercial-real-estate-lease) says a tenant improvement allowance is usually a set amount per square foot of rented space, and that landlords may offer rent-free months or turnkey work as inducements. We could not find a published per-square-foot allowance figure for Winnipeg, so treat any number as specific to that building and lease.

The allowance is often tied to lease length. Longer terms generally justify larger allowances, because they give the landlord more predictable income, according to [a tenant guide from PRG Real Estate](https://prgrealestate.ca/tenant-improvement-allowance-a-tenants-guide-for-commercial-leases/), a Greater Toronto brokerage.
Key terms to settle in the lease
**Who hires the contractor** and who approves drawings.
**The allowance amount** and what it can be spent on (construction only, or also design, permits, furniture).
**Who pays overruns** above the allowance.
**Schedule:** when work starts, when rent starts, and what happens if work runs late.
**Restoration:** does the tenant have to remove improvements at the end of the lease?
**Ownership:** attached improvements usually become the landlord's property unless the lease says otherwise.

[BDC](https://www.bdc.ca/en/articles-tools/money-finance/buy-lease-commercial-real-estate/how-to-protect-your-business-when-making-lease-hold-improvements) also advises getting the landlord's consent to your plans before signing. Our [commercial renovation financing guide](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank) lists more questions to ask about an allowance, and our [office fit-up guide](/blog/office-fit-up-lease-planning-winnipeg) lines the work up with your lease dates.
This is general information, not legal or financial advice. Have a commercial real estate lawyer review the lease.
Permits and code
Most TIs in Winnipeg need a City of Winnipeg building permit, though purely cosmetic work generally doesn't.

A new use (for example, office to clinic or retail to restaurant) is a change of use. It starts with a building permit application, then needs an occupancy permit before the space is used, and it may require upgrades for fire separation, exits, accessibility or plumbing.
Our guide to [occupancy permits and change of use](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) explains the steps. Factor permit review time into the move-in date.
Choosing a tenant improvement contractor in Winnipeg
Look for a contractor who:
Can talk through TIs like yours (office, retail, medical, restaurant) and give references
Gives a written scope and price after a site visit, so both sides know costs before signing the lease
Works around other tenants in the building, with clean, quiet, after-hours options
Coordinates permits and inspections

Checks out on public records. Search WCB Manitoba's clearance system, the Companies Office and the City's permit search, as our [contractor checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-contractor-for-your-renovation-project) explains
Tips for commercial agents
A written TI quote during negotiations helps both sides agree on the allowance and timeline. Bring a contractor in early, before the offer to lease is finalized.
The bottom line
Clear TI terms and a written scope and schedule help get tenants open on time and landlords paid on time.
